# Extension patterns: four archetypes {#sec:customization}

In plain terms: almost every extension you will write is one of four
**archetypes**. A **guard** watches and gates what Pi already does. A **tool**
gives the model one new capability. A **stateful extension** remembers things
correctly across reloads and branches. A **composer** coordinates tools,
sessions, and other extensions. The archetypes build on each other — a
stateful extension is a tool plus durable state, a composer is all three plus
coordination — so this chapter walks them in that order.

Each archetype is a **guided read of a real extension** shipped in the
repository (`packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/`), not an invented
scenario. Every code excerpt is followed by the *why*: the decision the
example's author made, and what goes wrong if you make the obvious
alternative. Open the full file beside the chapter — the path is named at the
start of each archetype.

Stop at the first archetype that covers your need. A mistake in a guard breaks
one tool call; a mistake in a composer can corrupt sessions.

```{mermaid}

```

This chapter is the production follow-up to [Your first
extension](#sec:extensions). Where that chapter built one demo extension, this
one teaches the patterns that make extensions survive real use.

## Prerequisites

Finish [Your first extension](#sec:extensions) first — this chapter assumes
you can write and load a one-file extension with `pi -e path/to/extension.ts`,
and that you know what a [hook](#sec:glossary), a session, and a slash
command are. A checkout of the `pi` repository is strongly recommended this
time: every archetype names its example file, and reading the full version
beside the excerpt is the intended workflow.

One mechanism check before the patterns: use **configuration** for a stable
value, an **extension** for behavior that reacts to events or needs Pi APIs,
and a **core change** only when every host must share the behavior.
[Customizing Pi](#sec:resources) is the canonical guide to that choice; the
rest of this chapter assumes you picked the middle row.

## Archetype 1 — The guard: watch and gate what Pi already does

A guard adds no commands and no tools. It subscribes to events with `pi.on()`
and occasionally says "no". That makes it the cheapest archetype to write and
the safest to get wrong — a bug breaks one operation, not your data. Across
the next three sections we grow one real file — `permission-gate.ts`, in
`packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/` — from its core idea to
production behavior, then look at a different event for the times you want
to steer instead of block.

### The example at a glance

**What it does:** `permission-gate.ts` watches every bash command the model
proposes and asks the user before running ones that match a dangerous
pattern (`rm -rf`, `sudo`, world-writable `chmod`). When nobody can answer
— print mode, JSON mode — it denies by default.

**Architecture:** one event handler, inserted at the one point in Pi's
pipeline where interception is cheap:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-guard-pipeline
%%| fig-cap: "Where a guard sits. tool_call fires after argument validation and before execution; returning block stops the call and the reason reaches the model as an error tool result."
%%| fig-width: 6.4
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"nodeSpacing": 10, "rankSpacing": 10}, "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "11px"}}}%%
flowchart LR
  M["Model proposes<br/>tool call"] --> V["Schema<br/>validation"]
  V --> G["tool_call handlers<br/>(the guard)"]
  G -->|allowed| X["Tool<br/>executes"]
  G -->|"block + reason"| E["Error result<br/>to the model"]
  X --> R["Result to<br/>the model"]
```

Every guard has the same anatomy — *subscribe* to an event, *filter* to the
calls it cares about, *return* a decision — and the three sections of this
archetype grow that anatomy: the core gate, the headless-mode policy that
keeps it safe everywhere, and a second event (`before_agent_start`) for
when you want to steer the model instead of blocking it.

### The simplest gate: listen, match, block

**Problem:** the model can propose destructive commands; you want a human in
the loop for the ones that match a policy.

**Recipe:** here is the complete shipped file. It is 34 lines, and every
guard you ever write will have this same three-part shape — *subscribe,
filter, return*:

```ts
// packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/permission-gate.ts
import type { ExtensionAPI } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent";

export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) {
  const dangerousPatterns = [/\brm\s+(-rf?|--recursive)/i, /\bsudo\b/i,
    /\b(chmod|chown)\b.*777/i];

  pi.on("tool_call", async (event, ctx) => {
    if (event.toolName !== "bash") return undefined;

    const command = event.input.command as string;
    const isDangerous = dangerousPatterns.some((p) => p.test(command));

    if (isDangerous) {
      if (!ctx.hasUI) {
        // In non-interactive mode, block by default
        return { block: true,
          reason: "Dangerous command blocked (no UI for confirmation)" };
      }

      const choice = await ctx.ui.select(
        `⚠️ Dangerous command:\n\n  ${command}\n\nAllow?`, ["Yes", "No"]);

      if (choice !== "Yes") {
        return { block: true, reason: "Blocked by user" };
      }
    }

    return undefined;
  });
}
```

Why each piece is shaped this way:

- **Subscribe:** `pi.on("tool_call", ...)` fires after the model's arguments
  have passed schema validation but *before* the tool runs. It is the last
  moment you can stop a call cheaply.
- **The return value is the whole protocol.** There is no `pi.skip()` or
  `next()` callback: `return undefined` means "no opinion, proceed", and
  `{ block: true, reason }` is the only denial signal. Handlers for the same
  event run in load order and each sees the previous handler's output — the
  first non-`undefined` result wins. If you forget the final
  `return undefined` it is harmless (`async` functions return `undefined`
  anyway), but writing it out keeps the protocol visible.
- **Filter first:** `if (event.toolName !== "bash") return undefined;` makes
  the handler free for every non-bash call. A guard that inspects every event
  it does not care about is a bug farm.
- **Regexes, not string equality:** `command === "rm -rf"` matches exactly one
  string; `\brm\s+(-rf?|--recursive)` catches `rm -rf /tmp/x`,
  `rm --recursive x`, and spacing variants. The `\b` word boundary keeps
  `grmbl` from matching. This is still heuristic — aliases, scripts, and
  obfuscation slip through. A gate raises the cost of accidents; it is not a
  sandbox.
- **`select(["Yes", "No"])` instead of `confirm`:** `confirm` collapses "user
  said no" and "user pressed Escape / walked away" into the same `false`.
  `select` returns the chosen string or `undefined` on cancel, so the guard
  can tell denial from abandonment. Here both deny — the `choice !== "Yes"`
  comparison treats anything but an explicit Yes as a no, which is the safe
  direction to collapse in.
- **The `reason` string is for the model, not the log.** A blocked call
  reaches the model as an error tool result containing your reason. A reason
  that says what happened ("Blocked by user") lets the model explain and
  propose an alternative instead of retrying blindly.

**Failure modes:**

- *Blocking is more honest than mutating.* `event.input` is mutable and later
  handlers see your changes, but Pi does not revalidate after a mutation —
  reserve mutation for narrow argument patches, not policy.
- *A throwing `tool_call` handler blocks the call* (fail-safe) and the error
  reaches the model as an error tool result. Test both the allow and deny
  paths.

**Verify:**

1. Run `pi -e .../permission-gate.ts` (the full shipped path) and ask Pi
   to remove a scratch directory with `rm -rf`. Observe: the
   dialog appears showing the exact command.
2. Choose "No". Observe: the command never runs, and the model receives
   `Blocked by user` as an error it responds to.
3. Ask for a harmless `ls`. Observe: no dialog, command runs normally.

### Survive headless mode: hasUI and timeouts

**Problem:** the gate above *asks the user* — but print and JSON modes have
no user, and an RPC client that never answers parks your handler forever. A
gate that hangs in RPC mode looks like a hung agent; a gate that silently
denies in print mode looks like a broken tool. Both are policy bugs, and you
fix them *before* writing the dialog, not after.

**Recipe:** two additions. First, decide the noninteractive policy up front —
the shipped file already does this, and now you can see why the check sits
where it does:

```ts
// permission-gate.ts — the check comes BEFORE any dialog call
if (!ctx.hasUI) {
  return { block: true,
    reason: "Dangerous command blocked (no UI for confirmation)" };
}
```

- `ctx.hasUI` is `false` in print and JSON modes, `true` in TUI and RPC
  modes (the full per-mode table is in [Your first
  extension](#sec:extensions)).
- Checking it *before* the dialog means `ctx.ui.select` is never even called
  on a host that cannot render it — no hang, no swallowed default, no crash
  inside dialog code.
- Denying when you cannot ask is **fail-closed**: the safe default for a
  destructive operation. (For a purely cosmetic gate you might fail open
  instead — the point is that the policy is a decision you make, not an
  accident of the mode.)

Second, bound every dialog so a silent client cannot wait forever.
`timed-confirm.ts` ships both variants:

```ts
// timed-confirm.ts — the simple variant: one option
const confirmed = await ctx.ui.confirm(
  "Dangerous command", "Allow this operation?",
  { timeout: 5000 }, // auto-cancels; confirm() returns false on timeout
);

// timed-confirm.ts — the manual variant, when you must tell
// "timed out" apart from "user said no":
const controller = new AbortController();
const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 5000);
const ok = await ctx.ui.confirm(
  "Confirm", "Proceed?", { signal: controller.signal });
clearTimeout(timeoutId);
// ok === false with controller.signal.aborted → timed out, not denied
```

- The `timeout` option is one argument and the right default; it collapses
  timeout and cancel into `false`, which is fine when both mean "deny".
- The `AbortSignal` variant exists for the cases where the difference
  matters — for example, logging "user denied" versus "no answer" in an
  audit trail. It mirrors the `fetch(url, { signal })` shape you already
  know.
- Require `ctx.mode === "tui"` (stricter than `hasUI`) for anything that
  needs a real terminal, like custom components.

**Verify:**

1. Run the gate under `pi -p -e ...` with a prompt that asks for `rm -rf`.
   Observe: the block reason mentions the missing UI, and the command never
   runs — no hang.
2. In the TUI, add `{ timeout: 2000 }` to the dialog and do not answer.
   Observe: after 2 seconds the dialog closes and the command is denied.
3. Use the `AbortSignal` variant, let it time out, and notify on
   `controller.signal.aborted`. Observe: the message says "timed out", not
   "cancelled by user".

### Steer, don't block: `before_agent_start`

**Problem:** sometimes you do not want to stop the model — you want it to
behave differently *before* it acts: prioritize correctness during reviews,
adapt to the user's tool configuration, or add project conventions. Blocking
is the wrong tool; you want to change what the model *sees*.

**Recipe:** choose the event by *when* you intervene. `tool_call` fires
*after* the model has decided (you gate the decision). `before_agent_start`
fires once per prompt, *before* the agent loop starts (you steer the
decision). `prompt-customizer.ts` uses it to append tool-specific guidance
that adapts to whatever tools and skills are actually active:

```ts
// packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/prompt-customizer.ts (excerpt)
export default function promptCustomizer(pi: ExtensionAPI) {
  pi.on("before_agent_start", async (event) => {
    const { systemPrompt, systemPromptOptions } = event;

    const customPrompt = addToolGuidance(systemPromptOptions, systemPrompt);
    const appendSection = mergeWithUserAppend(systemPromptOptions);

    return {
      systemPrompt: `${customPrompt}${appendSection}`,
    };
  });
}
```

- **Append, never replace.** `event.systemPrompt` already contains Pi's
  built-in instructions, skills, context files, and the user's own appended
  prompts. Returning a brand-new string discards all of it; returning
  `systemPrompt + myGuidance` keeps it.
- **`event.systemPromptOptions` is why this example adapts.** Instead of
  hardcoding "use the read tool", `addToolGuidance` reads
  `systemPromptOptions.selectedTools` and `systemPromptOptions.skills` and
  only writes guidance for what is actually configured. If the user disabled
  `edit`, the guidance for `edit` disappears too.
- You can also return `{ message: { customType, content, display } }` to
  inject a one-off message for this prompt instead of editing the system
  prompt. `display` controls transcript visibility only — the model receives
  the message either way. (`plan-mode/`, which you will meet in archetype 4,
  uses `display: false` for machine-only instructions.)
- The boundary with the `context` event, in one sentence:
  `before_agent_start` runs once per prompt; `context` runs before *every*
  provider request (including retries and tool-call follow-ups) and can
  rewrite the whole message list. [The prompt lifecycle](#sec:prompt-lifecycle)
  has the full picture when you need it.

**Failure mode:** replacing the system prompt instead of appending discards
skills, tools, context files, and user-provided instructions. Prefer a
narrow, conditional append.

**Verify:**

1. Run `pi -e .../prompt-customizer.ts` and ask any question. Observe: the
   behavior follows your appended guidance.
2. Compare a run with the extension and one without. Observe: only the
   extension's run reflects the guidance.
3. If you returned a `message` with `display: true`, check the transcript:
   the injected message is visible there.

**More guards to study:** `protected-paths.ts` (blocks writes to `.env`,
`.git/`, `node_modules/`), `confirm-destructive.ts` (gates session
operations), `dirty-repo-guard.ts` (gates on git state).

## Archetype 2 — The tool: give the model one real capability

You built a minimal tool in [Your first extension](#sec:extensions) (`name`,
`label`, `description`, TypeBox `parameters`, `execute` returning
`content`/`details`). This archetype is what makes a tool survive real use,
told as a guided read of one real file: `truncated-tool.ts`, in
`packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/`.

### The example at a glance

**What it does:** `truncated-tool.ts` wraps ripgrep as an `rg` tool the
model can call. The problem it solves: raw search output is unbounded — one
`rg` call can return more text than fits in the model's context window —
and a naive wrapper would flood the context, confuse errors with empty
results, and leave the human staring at raw JSON.

**Architecture:** the file is a pipeline of layers, each answering one
question:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-tool-pipeline
%%| fig-cap: "truncated-tool.ts as a pipeline. Each layer answers one question; the sections of this archetype read them in order."
%%| fig-width: 6.4
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"nodeSpacing": 10, "rankSpacing": 10}, "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "11px"}}}%%
flowchart LR
  S["Schema<br/>what may the<br/>model ask?"] --> X["Execute<br/>run rg, capture<br/>everything"]
  X --> E["Errors<br/>expected outcome<br/>or real failure?"]
  E --> T["Truncate<br/>what fits in<br/>context?"]
  T --> R["Render<br/>what does the<br/>human see?"]
```

The sections below read the file one layer at a time, in pipeline order:
the schema the model reads, the command that runs, the error paths, the
output limits, and the transcript rendering. The sixth layer — the
file-safety queue — is not a pipeline stage but a cross-cutting guard
around every file write the tool makes, so it comes last.

### Schema first: what the model reads

**Problem:** the model never sees your code. Everything it knows about your
tool comes from the name, the `description`, and the `parameters` schema —
so those strings *are* your tool's documentation.

**Recipe:** the top of `truncated-tool.ts`:

```ts
// truncated-tool.ts (lines 33-37, 53-54)
const RgParams = Type.Object({
  pattern: Type.String({ description: "Search pattern (regex)" }),
  path: Type.Optional(Type.String({
    description: "Directory to search (default: current directory)",
  })),
  glob: Type.Optional(Type.String({
    description: "File glob pattern, e.g. '*.ts'",
  })),
});

// ...inside pi.registerTool({ ... }):
description: `Search file contents using ripgrep. Output is truncated to
${DEFAULT_MAX_LINES} lines or ${formatSize(DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES)} (whichever is
hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file.`,
parameters: RgParams,
```

- **Every field `description` is read by the model** when it decides
  argument values. `description: "File glob pattern, e.g. '*.ts'"` is what
  teaches the model to pass `--glob '*.ts'` rather than embedding the glob
  in the pattern.
- **The tool-level `description` sets expectations, not just purpose.**
  Stating the truncation limits up front teaches the model to make
  reasonable requests — and, crucially, that when output is truncated it
  should *read the temp file* instead of re-running the search with a
  narrower pattern. You will see where the temp file comes from in the
  truncation layer below; the description is the promise, the
  implementation is the delivery.
- **`Type.Optional(...)` is a model-facing signal too**: it tells the model
  the parameter can be omitted, and the parenthetical default
  (`(default: current directory)`) tells it what omitting means.

#### StringEnum vs Type.Union for string literals {#stringenum-vs-typeunion-for-string-literals}

When a parameter is a choice from a fixed set of strings, reach for
`StringEnum` from `@earendil-works/pi-ai` — not
`Type.Union([Type.Literal("a"), Type.Literal("b")])`. The reason is concrete.
The two forms generate different JSON Schema for the provider:

```ts
import { StringEnum } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai";

// StringEnum(["small", "large"]) emits the plain enum form:
//   { "type": "string", "enum": ["small", "large"] }

// Type.Union([Type.Literal("small"), Type.Literal("large")]) emits:
//   { "anyOf": [{ "const": "small" }, { "const": "large" }] }
```

Every provider understands the plain `enum` form. Google's Gemini API rejects
the `anyOf`/`const` representation, and when the schema is rejected the model
may emit values your schema never intended. The rule is simple: **always
`StringEnum` for string choices.** `todo.ts` — the next archetype's anchor —
builds its entire tool around one:
`action: StringEnum(["list", "add", "toggle", "clear"] as const)`.

**Verify:**

1. Load the tool and prompt: `use rg to find the word ExtensionAPI in
   TypeScript files`. Observe: the model passes a `glob`, because the schema
   taught it the parameter exists.
2. Remove a field `description`, reload, and repeat. Observe: the model's
   arguments get sloppier — that string was doing real work.

### Execute core: run the command {#tool-execute-core}

**Problem:** your tool wraps a real program. The core loop is: build the
command, run it, capture *everything*, decide what kind of outcome each exit
path represents.

**Recipe:** the heart of the tool:

```ts
// truncated-tool.ts (excerpt from execute, lines 56-81)
const args = ["rg", "--line-number", "--color=never"];
if (glob) args.push("--glob", glob);
args.push(pattern);
args.push(searchPath || ".");

let output: string;
try {
  output = execSync(args.join(" "), {
    cwd: ctx.cwd,
    encoding: "utf-8",
    maxBuffer: 100 * 1024 * 1024, // 100MB buffer to capture full output
  });
} catch (err: any) {
  // ripgrep exits with 1 when no matches found
  if (err.status === 1) {
    return {
      content: [{ type: "text", text: "No matches found" }],
      details: { pattern, path: searchPath, glob, matchCount: 0 },
    };
  }
  throw new Error(`ripgrep failed: ${err.message}`);
}
```

- **`cwd: ctx.cwd`** runs the search in the project the user opened Pi in,
  not wherever the Pi process happened to start. Resolve every relative
  path from `ctx.cwd` for the same reason.
- **`maxBuffer: 100MB` is deliberate.** The tool captures the *complete*
  output into memory so it can count the real totals and save the full text
  to a file — truncation happens *after* capture, not in the pipe. (This is
  a memory tradeoff; it is what makes the exact "showing X of Y lines"
  notice possible.)
- **Exit code 1 is not an error.** ripgrep uses it for "no matches" — an
  expected outcome the model can act on — so the tool returns a normal
  result with `matchCount: 0` in `details`. The next section turns this
  into a general rule.
- **`--color=never`** because ANSI color codes would pollute the text the
  model reads.

> **Spot the bug — Esc cannot stop this tool.** `execute` receives an
> `AbortSignal` (`_signal` here, unused) that fires when the user presses
> Esc. `execSync` blocks the event loop and *ignores* the signal entirely,
> so a 30-second search cannot be cancelled. The example chose simplicity;
> a production tool should use async `spawn`/`exec` and forward the signal
> so Esc kills the child process. Whenever your tool calls out to something
> long-running — `fetch`, a subprocess, a heavy computation — forwarding
> `signal` is the difference between "Esc works" and "Esc does nothing".

**Verify:**

1. Prompt for a search with many matches. Observe: results come back with
   line numbers, no color garbage.
2. Prompt for a pattern that matches nothing. Observe: the model reports
   "no matches" — it got a normal result, not an error to diagnose.

### Error paths: the throw-vs-return decision rule

**Problem:** "the tool failed" and "the tool succeeded with an empty answer"
look identical if you only return text. The model handles them very
differently.

**Decision rule, stated once:** *if the outcome is an expected state the
model can act on, return it as a normal result; if something broke and
retrying with the same input will not help, throw.*

- **Return** for expected outcomes: no matches, an empty file, a valid but
  empty list. The model reads the result and moves on.
- **Throw** for real failures: ripgrep not installed, an unreadable
  directory, an invalid flag. Pi catches the throw and delivers an
  `isError: true` tool result to the model, which treats it as "the tool is
  broken" rather than "the answer is empty".
- **Never return a field named `isError`** on the result object — Pi
  ignores it. Throwing is the only error channel. (The empty-output guard
  later in the file — `if (!output.trim())` — is handled exactly like exit
  code 1, because an empty successful run *is* "no matches".)

**Verify:**

1. Search a pattern with no matches and then open the session file
   (`~/.pi/agent/sessions/...`). Observe: the tool result entry carries
   `details: { matchCount: 0, ... }` — structured outcomes are persisted,
   not just the text. (Remember this; archetype 3 is built on it.)
2. Point the tool at a nonexistent directory. Observe: the model receives
   an error result and reports the failure instead of inventing output.

### Truncation: why Pi doesn't do it for you

**Problem:** a search can return megabytes. If all of it goes into the
model's context, one tool call can blow the window. The beginner's question
is *why doesn't Pi just truncate my output?* — and the answer is the whole
pattern: **Pi cannot know which part of your output matters** (the first
matches? the last log lines?) or where the rest should go. Only you know
that, so custom tool output is *not* automatically truncated.

**Recipe:** the middle of `execute`:

```ts
// truncated-tool.ts (excerpt, lines 91-120)
const truncation = truncateHead(output, {
  maxLines: DEFAULT_MAX_LINES,
  maxBytes: DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES,
});

const details: RgDetails = { pattern, path: searchPath, glob, matchCount };
let resultText = truncation.content;

if (truncation.truncated) {
  const tempDir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), "pi-rg-"));
  const tempFile = join(tempDir, "output.txt");
  await withFileMutationQueue(tempFile, async () => {
    await writeFile(tempFile, output, "utf8");
  });

  details.truncation = truncation;
  details.fullOutputPath = tempFile;

  resultText += `\n\n[Output truncated: showing ${truncation.outputLines}` +
    ` of ${truncation.totalLines} lines. Full output saved to: ${tempFile}]`;
}

return { content: [{ type: "text", text: resultText }], details };
```

- **`truncateHead` keeps the beginning** — right for search results, where
  the first matches matter most. `truncateTail` keeps the end — right for
  logs and command output, where the latest lines matter. Choosing the
  direction is exactly the knowledge Pi doesn't have.
- **`DEFAULT_MAX_LINES` (2,000) and `DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES` (50 KB) match Pi's
  built-in tools.** Using the same limits keeps behavior predictable across
  tools; `formatSize()` renders the byte counts human-readably.
- **The full output goes to a temp file, and the model is told the exact
  counts and the path.** A model cannot use a file it does not know about;
  the `[Output truncated: ...]` notice turns "missing data" into "data
  available on request" — the model can call `read` on the temp file if it
  needs more.
- **`details` carries the machine-readable version** (`truncation`,
  `fullOutputPath`) so the renderer — next layer — can display "17 matches
  (truncated)" without re-parsing the text.

**Verify:**

1. Search a common word across the repo (guaranteed >2,000 lines). Observe:
   the result ends with the truncation notice and a temp-file path.
2. Ask the model a question about the omitted matches. Observe: it reads
   the temp file instead of re-running the search.
3. Search something rare. Observe: no notice, `truncation.truncated` is
   false, content untouched.

### Rendering: compact call, scannable result

**Problem:** the model consumes `content`; the *human* consumes the
transcript. Without renderers, the human sees raw JSON arguments and a wall
of result text.

**Recipe:** the renderer contract, which the tutorial never covered. Both
hooks are optional — omit them and Pi falls back to a default
`name: result` display:

```ts
// truncated-tool.ts (excerpt, lines 138-152, 155-172)
renderCall(args, theme, _context) {
  let text = theme.fg("toolTitle", theme.bold("rg "));
  text += theme.fg("accent", `"${args.pattern}"`);
  if (args.path) text += theme.fg("muted", ` in ${args.path}`);
  if (args.glob) text += theme.fg("dim", ` --glob ${args.glob}`);
  return new Text(text, 0, 0);
},

renderResult(result, { expanded, isPartial }, theme, _context) {
  const details = result.details as RgDetails | undefined;

  if (isPartial) {
    return new Text(theme.fg("warning", "Searching..."), 0, 0);
  }
  if (!details || details.matchCount === 0) {
    return new Text(theme.fg("dim", "No matches found"), 0, 0);
  }
  // collapsed: "17 matches" (+ "(truncated)" warning)
  // expanded: first ~20 lines + "Full output: <temp file>" hint
  // ...
},
```

- **`renderCall` is one compact line.** The human needs `rg "pattern" in
  src`, not the full argument JSON — the model already has the arguments.
- **`renderResult` branches on the state the tool can be in.** `isPartial`
  is true while results stream in (show progress, not garbage);
  `matchCount === 0` gets a dim one-liner; truncation adds a warning tag;
  `expanded` (the user toggles it in the TUI) reveals the first ~20 lines
  plus the temp-file hint.
- **The renderer reads `details`, never `content`.** Everything it needs —
  counts, truncation state, temp path — was put into `details` during
  `execute`. That is why the earlier layers bothered with structured
  details: rendering, persistence, and state recovery all read the same
  object.

**Verify:**

1. Run a search and look at the collapsed result. Observe: one line,
   `N matches`, with `(truncated)` when applicable.
2. Expand the result in the TUI. Observe: the first ~20 match lines and the
   full-output path.
3. Run a slow search and watch during execution. Observe: the partial
   "Searching..." state.

### File queue: serializing same-file mutations {#serialize-same-file-mutations}

**Problem:** tool calls run in parallel by default. If your custom tool
edits `foo.ts` while built-in `edit` also changes `foo.ts` in the same
turn, both read the original and whichever write lands last silently wins —
one edit is gone with no error anywhere.

**Recipe:** `withFileMutationQueue()`, the per-path async queue the built-in
`edit` and `write` tools already use. You saw it in the truncation layer
wrapping the temp-file write; the general pattern wraps the *entire*
read-modify-write window:

```ts
import { withFileMutationQueue } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent";
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { resolve } from "node:path";

// Inside a tool's execute():
const absolutePath = resolve(ctx.cwd, params.path);

await withFileMutationQueue(absolutePath, async () => {
  const current = await readFile(absolutePath, "utf8");
  await writeFile(absolutePath, update(current));
});
```

- **The queue key is the canonical path.** For existing files the helper
  canonicalizes through `realpath()`, so `foo.ts` and a symlink alias of it
  share one queue. Resolve the path from `ctx.cwd` *first* and use that
  same absolute path for the queue and every file operation inside it.
- **Different files still run in parallel** — the queue serializes per
  path, so it costs you nothing on unrelated files.
- **The temp-file write in the anchor is the simple case; the read-modify-
  write race with built-in `edit` is the real one.** Wrap the whole window,
  not just the write: if the read happens outside the queue, you can still
  lose the sibling's edit.

**Verify:**

1. Ask the model to make two edits to the same file in one turn using your
   queued tool and built-in `edit`. Observe: both changes are present.
2. Repeat through a symlink to the file. Observe: still both changes — the
  canonicalized queue key merged the aliases.

## Archetype 3 — The stateful extension: remember things correctly

A stateful extension is a tool (archetype 2) plus memory. The anchor is
`todo.ts` from the shipped examples: a `todo` tool the model calls and a
`/todos` command for the user, with a list that survives `/reload`, restart,
and branching.

### The example at a glance

**What it does:** `todo.ts` gives the model a `todo` tool (list, add,
toggle, clear) and the user a `/todos` command that opens a full-screen
list. The list survives `/reload`, process restart, `/fork`, and `/tree`
navigation — always matching the branch you are looking at.

**Architecture:** two data flows plus a UI layer — which are exactly the
three passes of this archetype:

- **Write path (pass 1):** every `execute` call — including errors — stores
  a complete snapshot of the list in its tool result's `details`. Pi
  persists tool results into the session file, so the session itself
  becomes the database.
- **Read path (pass 2):** on `session_start` and `session_tree`, the
  extension walks the active branch with `getBranch()` and rebuilds its
  in-memory variables from the snapshots.
- **UI layer (pass 3):** `renderCall`/`renderResult` keep tool results
  compact in the transcript, and `/todos` renders a custom component for
  the user.

One requirement drives every design choice in this file, so state it before
the code: in [Your first extension](#sec:extensions) the greeting counter
was *session-wide* on purpose — it rebuilt from `getEntries()`, every entry
in the file. A todo list is different: when you `/fork` to try an experiment
and `/tree`-navigate back, the list must match the branch you are looking
at. **Branch-correctness is the requirement; everything below — snapshots in
tool results, the rebuild loop, the two events — follows from it.**

### Pass 1: the tool and its snapshot-per-result design

**Problem:** tool results are already persisted in the session file. If each
result carried the whole state, the session *itself* would be the database —
no side files, nothing extra to sync.

**Recipe:** every branch of `execute` — including `list`, and including
*every error path* — returns the complete state in `details`:

```ts
// todo.ts (excerpt from execute's "add" branch)
const newTodo: Todo = { id: nextId++, text: params.text, done: false };
todos.push(newTodo);
return {
  content: [{ type: "text",
    text: `Added todo #${newTodo.id}: ${newTodo.text}` }],
  details: { action: "add", todos: [...todos], nextId },
};

// and even validation failures carry the full state:
//   details: { action: "add", todos: [...todos], nextId,
//     error: "text required" }
```

- **`todos: [...todos]` is a copy, not a reference.** If the result held the
  live array, later mutations would retroactively rewrite what was already
  persisted — the stored history would lie about what the state was at that
  point.
- **Error results snapshot too.** If an error path omitted `details`, a
  rebuild that walks results in order would silently drop state at the
  first failed call. Snapshot-everything makes rebuilds robust regardless
  of which path executed.
- **The snapshot replaces, never merges.** Each result stores the *entire*
  list, so the most recent result *is* the current state — no replaying
  deltas, no "add #5, remove #3" algebra that breaks when entries are
  compacted or reordered.
- **`details` must be JSON-serializable.** It lives in the session file:
  no functions, `Map`s, `Date`s, or circular references — those silently
  vanish or corrupt on write.

### Pass 2: the rebuild loop {#state-that-survives-restart-and-branching}

**Problem:** anything your extension keeps in a variable disappears when Pi
reloads, restarts, resumes, or forks. The snapshots from pass 1 are durable;
this pass is the loop that rebuilds the variables from them.

**Recipe:** one function, wired to two events:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-state-rebuild
%%| fig-cap: "Durable state loop, as implemented by todo.ts. Each tool call stores a snapshot in its result's details, which Pi persists as a session entry. On session_start and again on session_tree (branch navigation), the extension walks getBranch() and rebuilds its in-memory state from the snapshots."
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"nodeSpacing": 16, "rankSpacing": 16}, "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "12px"}}}%%
flowchart TD
  D["Serializable<br/>tool-result details"] --> E["Durable<br/>session entry"]
  E --> B["Scan active branch<br/>root to leaf"]
  T["session_start /<br/>session_tree"] --> B
  B --> R["Rebuild in-memory<br/>state"]
```

```ts
// todo.ts (excerpt, lightly simplified)
let todos: Todo[] = [];
let nextId = 1;

const reconstructState = (ctx: ExtensionContext) => {
  todos = [];
  nextId = 1;
  for (const entry of ctx.sessionManager.getBranch()) {
    if (entry.type !== "message") continue;
    const msg = entry.message;
    if (msg.role !== "toolResult" || msg.toolName !== "todo") continue;
    const details = msg.details as TodoDetails | undefined;
    if (details) {
      todos = details.todos;
      nextId = details.nextId;
    }
  }
};

pi.on("session_start", async (_event, ctx) => reconstructState(ctx));
pi.on("session_tree", async (_event, ctx) => reconstructState(ctx));
```

- **Reset first, then apply in order.** `todos = []; nextId = 1;` before the
  scan is mandatory: anything retained from before the rebuild mixes the
  branch you *left* into the branch you are on. Inside the loop,
  `todos = details.todos` is a wholesale replacement, so the last matching
  result on the branch wins — exactly the semantics pass 1 designed for.
- **`getBranch()`, not `getEntries()` — this is the decision the whole
  archetype hangs on.** The session is a tree of entries; `getEntries()`
  returns *all* of them, including dead siblings from forks you abandoned,
  so a rebuild from it mixes branches together. `getBranch()` follows
  parent pointers from the active leaf to the root — only what is actually
  on this conversation's history. (Full session semantics: [Sessions,
  branches, and durable context](#sec:sessions).)
- **Two events because they cover disjoint paths.** `session_start` fires
  on initial load, `/fork`, and `pi --resume` (with `reason: "fork"` /
  `"resume"`). `session_tree` fires when `/tree` navigation moves the
  active branch inside a *running* session. Subscribe to only one and
  either restart or navigation leaves stale state behind.

**Verify** (a full lifecycle script):

1. `pi -e .../todo.ts`, then:
   `add three todos: buy milk, write docs, review PR`. Observe: three
   `✓ Added` lines.
2. `/reload`, then `list my todos`. Observe: all three survive —
   `session_start` rebuilt them.
3. `/fork`, then `add a todo: experiment`, then `list my todos`. Observe:
   four todos on the fork.
4. `/tree`-navigate back to the parent, then `list my todos`. Observe:
   "experiment" is *gone* — `session_tree` rebuilt from this branch only.
5. Navigate forward to the fork again. Observe: "experiment" is back.
6. Quit, then `pi --resume`, and list. Observe: state matches where you
   left it — `session_start` with `reason: "resume"` rebuilt it.

### Pass 3: the human layer

**Problem:** the state loop is invisible machinery. Users still need to
*see* the list — compact tool results in the transcript, and a full view on
demand.

**Recipe:** the half of `todo.ts` the previous passes skipped.

- **`renderCall` / `renderResult`** (same contract as archetype 2): the
  transcript shows `✓ Added #3 buy milk` or a 5-item collapsed list with an
  expand toggle, instead of raw JSON. The renderer reads `details` — which
  is always present and always complete, thanks to pass 1.
- **The `/todos` command renders a custom component — guarded:**

```ts
// todo.ts (excerpt)
pi.registerCommand("todos", {
  description: "Show all todos on the current branch",
  handler: async (_args, ctx) => {
    if (ctx.mode !== "tui") {
      ctx.ui.notify("/todos requires interactive mode", "error");
      return;
    }
    await ctx.ui.custom<void>((_tui, theme, _kb, done) =>
      new TodoListComponent(todos, theme, () => done()));
  },
});
```

  `ctx.ui.custom` needs a real terminal; in print/JSON/RPC modes it would
  throw or hang. The `ctx.mode !== "tui"` guard — stricter than `hasUI`
  from archetype 1 — turns a crash into a clear message. Any command that
  opens custom UI needs this guard.
- **The component caches its rendered lines** (`cachedLines`, invalidated
  when the width changes) because the TUI re-renders on every keystroke;
  recomputing strings per frame is input lag you can feel.

**Verify:**

1. `list my todos` and look at the transcript. Observe: a formatted list
   with checkmarks, not JSON.
2. Run `/todos`. Observe: a bordered component with a `done/total` header;
   Escape closes it.
3. Run `pi -e todo.ts -p "list my todos"` (print mode) and try `/todos` in
   an RPC client. Observe: the guard message, not a crash.

### Who sees what: messages, entries, and delivery {#messages-entries-and-delivery-modes}

**Problem:** you need to put something into the session. There are three
APIs, and they differ in *who sees the payload* and *when it lands* —
choose wrong and the model sees your bookkeeping, or your urgent message
sits in a queue while the agent idles.

**Decision table:**

| API | Model sees it? | User sees it? | Starts a turn? | While streaming |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sendMessage()` | Yes | Only with `display: true` | Only with `triggerTurn: true` | Safe; default queue is `"steer"` |
| `appendEntry()` | No | Only with `registerEntryRenderer()` | No | Always safe |
| `sendUserMessage()` | Yes, as a user message | Yes | Always | Throws without `deliverAs` |

**The rules behind the table:**

1. **Information for the model → `pi.sendMessage()`.** Never use it for
   private bookkeeping — the model receives everything you send. While the
   agent is *idle*, a plain `sendMessage()` only appends to a queue;
   `triggerTurn: true` is what actually wakes the agent. `file-trigger.ts`
   uses exactly this to let an external system start work by writing a
   file:

```ts
// file-trigger.ts (excerpt, inside a fs.watch callback)
pi.sendMessage(
  { customType: "file-trigger",
    content: `External trigger: ${content}`,
    display: true },
  { triggerTurn: true }, // wake the agent even when idle
);
fs.writeFileSync(triggerFile, ""); // clear so the same file can trigger again
```

   The `deliverAs` option picks the queue: `"steer"` (default) redirects
   work in progress, `"followUp"` runs after the current run would
   otherwise stop, `"nextTurn"` attaches to the next user prompt without
   starting anything. Drain-point details are in [Stage 4 of the prompt
   lifecycle](#sec:prompt-lifecycle).

2. **Durable data for the user only → `pi.appendEntry()` + a renderer.**
   The model never sees entries; without a renderer they are invisible in
   the transcript too (but still persisted). `entry-renderer.ts` is the
   complete minimal pairing — a `/status-card` command that appends, and a
   renderer that draws the card:

```ts
// entry-renderer.ts (excerpt)
pi.registerEntryRenderer<StatusCardData>("status-card",
  (entry, { expanded }, theme) => {
    const data = entry.data ?? { message: "No data", timestamp: Date.now() };
    const box = new Box(1, 1, (t) => theme.bg("customMessageBg", t));
    const label = `${theme.fg("accent", "[status]")} ${data.message}`;
    box.addChild(new Text(label, 0, 0));
    return box;
  });

pi.registerCommand("status-card", {
  description: "Render a durable status card that is not sent to the LLM",
  handler: async (args) => {
    pi.appendEntry<StatusCardData>("status-card",
      { message: args.trim() || "Status card", timestamp: Date.now() });
  },
});
```

3. **A genuine user message → `pi.sendUserMessage()`.** It always starts or
   continues a turn, and while the agent is streaming you *must* pass
   `deliverAs: "steer"` or `"followUp"` — omitting it throws, because there
   is no safe default between interrupting and waiting. That is why
   `send-user-message.ts` guards with `ctx.isIdle()` before the plain call
   and branches to the `deliverAs` forms while busy.

4. **Never start a second direct agent run from a hook.** These queues are
   the supported way to inject work.

> **Spot the bug — `file-trigger.ts` leaks its watcher.** The watcher is
> created inside `session_start` and never closed. Every `/reload` fires
> `session_start` again, adding *another* `fs.watch` on the same file — and
> each stale watcher holds the old instance's `pi`, so a trigger can be
> delivered twice (or through a dead runtime). The fix is the lifecycle
> pair you will see again in the composer's event-bus pattern:

```ts
// Fixed shape: keep a handle, close on shutdown, defensively close on start
let watcher: fs.FSWatcher | undefined;

pi.on("session_start", () => {
  watcher?.close(); // defensive: drop any prior watcher
  watcher = fs.watch(triggerFile, () => { /* ... */ });
});

pi.on("session_shutdown", () => {
  watcher?.close();
  watcher = undefined;
});
```

**Verify:**

1. Run `file-trigger.ts`, then from another terminal
   `echo "Run the tests" > /tmp/agent-trigger.txt`. Observe: the idle agent
   wakes and responds (`triggerTurn` at work).
2. Comment out `triggerTurn: true`, reload, repeat. Observe: nothing
   happens until you submit a prompt yourself.
3. `/status-card deploy green` with `entry-renderer.ts` loaded. Observe: a
   colored card in the transcript; then ask the model what the card said —
   it does not know.
4. With the *unfixed* `file-trigger.ts`: `/reload` twice, then trigger the
   file. Observe duplicate deliveries; apply the fix and confirm exactly
   one.

## Archetype 4 — The composer: coordinate tools, sessions, and extensions

A composer combines the previous archetypes into a working mode, workflow,
or multi-extension system. The capstone is a guided tour of `plan-mode/`
in the shipped examples, because almost all of it is patterns you have
already seen, assembled with intent.

### The example at a glance

**What it does:** `plan-mode/` implements a read-only planning mode.
Toggle it on and the model can explore — `read`, search tools, an
allowlisted subset of `bash` — but cannot change anything (`edit`/`write`
are removed). When the model produces a numbered plan, the user can execute
it with live progress tracking (`[DONE:n]` markers and a widget), and the
whole mode survives `/reload` and resume.

**Architecture:** six cooperating subsystems. The tour walks them in this
order, and the right column says where you already learned each pattern:

| # | Subsystem | Pattern source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mode toggle + tool-set save/restore | New: `getActiveTools()` / `setActiveTools()` |
| 2 | Bash allowlist gate | Archetype 1 (`tool_call` block) |
| 3 | Mode persistence | Archetype 3 (`appendEntry`, session-wide) |
| 4 | Resume reconstruction | New: a marker entry bounding the history scan |
| 5 | Status line + widget | ch07 UI surfaces, rebuilt from state |
| 6 | Execution kickoff | Archetype 3 delivery (`followUp` + `triggerTurn`) |

After the tour, four standalone patterns cover what plan-mode does not:
dynamic tool loading, session replacement, inter-extension events, and tool
overrides.

### The plan-mode tour {#the-plan-mode-tour}

#### 1. Mode toggle + save/restore (new: the active tool set)

**Problem:** plan mode needs the model to have *fewer* tools (no `edit`/`write`),
without breaking anything else the user has loaded.

```ts
// plan-mode/index.ts (excerpt)
let toolsBeforePlanMode: string[] | undefined;
const PLAN_MODE_DISABLED_TOOLS = new Set(["edit", "write"]);

function enablePlanModeTools(): void {
  if (toolsBeforePlanMode === undefined) {
    toolsBeforePlanMode = pi.getActiveTools(); // save ONCE, on entry
  }
  pi.setActiveTools(getPlanModeTools(toolsBeforePlanMode));
}

function restoreNormalModeTools(): void {
  pi.setActiveTools(
    toolsBeforePlanMode ?? getNormalModeTools(pi.getActiveTools()));
  toolsBeforePlanMode = undefined;
}
```

- **Save once, on entry.** If you re-read `getActiveTools()` on every
  toggle, a tool activated *during* plan mode would be silently dropped on
  exit. The `undefined` guard makes the entry snapshot sticky.
- **Filter + union, never hardcode.** `getPlanModeTools` removes the
  disabled names from the saved selection and unions in plan-mode extras —
  so tools from *other extensions* survive the mode switch. A hardcoded
  `setActiveTools(["read", "bash"])` would destroy every other extension's
  tools; it is also a real model-policy change (it rebuilds the system
  prompt), not a UI filter — which is why plan mode signals the switch with
  a status indicator (subsystem 5).
- **Restore exactly what you saved**, then clear the snapshot so the next
  entry saves fresh. `preset.ts` uses the same save/restore discipline for
  named presets.

#### 2. The bash allowlist (archetype 1, reused)

```ts
// plan-mode/index.ts (excerpt)
pi.on("tool_call", async (event) => {
  if (!planModeEnabled || event.toolName !== "bash") return;

  const command = event.input.command as string;
  if (!isSafeCommand(command)) {
    return {
      block: true,
      reason: `Plan mode: command blocked (not allowlisted).` +
        ` Use /plan to disable plan mode first.\nCommand: ${command}`,
    };
  }
});
```

Same event, same `{ block, reason }` protocol as `permission-gate.ts` — the
new lesson is in the `reason` string: **it tells the model how to leave the
mode.** Without "Use /plan to disable plan mode first", the model knows it
was blocked but not what to do about it, and retries the same command in a
loop. A good block reason always contains the next action.

#### 3. Persistence (archetype 3, reused — with the other durability choice)

`togglePlanMode` ends with `persistState()`, which is simply a
`pi.appendEntry("plan-mode", { ... })` of the whole state object, and
`session_start` restores the latest entry. Two things to notice:

- **`persistState()` runs after *every* mutation** — toggle, step
  completion, execution finish — not just on exit. There is no "save"
  moment in a session you can `/reload` at any time; durability means
  writing at the moment of change. (The file even carries the comment
  *"Save cleared state so resume doesn't restore old execution mode"* —
  the author was bitten by exactly this.)
- **plan-mode deliberately uses `appendEntry` + `getEntries()`**, the
  session-wide choice from the ch07 counter — because "is plan mode on" is
  metadata about the *session*, not conversation content that should fork
  with branches. todo.ts used `details` + `getBranch()` because todos
  belong to the conversation. Choosing between them is now a decision you
  can make deliberately: *does this state belong to the session, or to the
  branch?*

#### 4. Resume reconstruction (the subtle one)

**Problem:** during execution, the model marks completed steps with
`[DONE:n]` tags in its messages. On resume, plan-mode re-scans assistant
messages to rebuild step completion — but a *previous* plan's `[DONE:n]`
tags are still in the history, and counting them would corrupt the new
execution's progress.

**Recipe:** a marker entry. When execution starts, plan-mode sends the
kickoff message with `customType: "plan-mode-execute"`. On resume, the
re-scan starts *after the last such marker*:

```ts
// plan-mode/index.ts (excerpt from session_start)
// Find the index of the last plan-mode-execute entry (marks when the
// current execution started)
let executeIndex = -1;
for (let i = entries.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
  if (entries[i].customType === "plan-mode-execute") {
    executeIndex = i;
    break;
  }
}

// Only scan messages AFTER the execute marker
for (let i = executeIndex + 1; i < entries.length; i++) {
  const entry = entries[i];
  if (entry.type === "message" && isAssistantMessage(entry.message)) {
    messages.push(entry.message);
  }
}
markCompletedSteps(messages.map(getTextContent).join("\n"), todoItems);
```

The general pattern: **when you reconstruct by scanning history, define the
boundary of "history that counts" explicitly** — a marker entry, a
timestamp, a session boundary — or old data will leak into new state.

#### 5. UI affordances (status, widget, and why `display: false`)

`updateStatus(ctx)` maintains a footer status (`⏸ plan`, `📋 2/5`) and a
todo widget via `ctx.ui.setStatus` / `ctx.ui.setWidget`, and is called after
every state mutation — the UI is *rebuilt from state*, never mutated
independently, so a `/reload` (which rebuilds state in `session_start` and
then calls `updateStatus`) leaves the indicators correct. Meanwhile the
mode instructions injected via `before_agent_start` use `display: false`:
they exist for the model only, and printing them would fight the UI's own
indicators with a second, textual source of truth. Rule of thumb: *the user
learns the mode from the status line; the model learns it from the injected
message; never show the model's instructions as if they were UI.*

#### 6. Execution kickoff (`deliverAs` + `triggerTurn`, together)

When the user picks "Execute the plan" in a dialog, no user message is
typed — but the model must start working. plan-mode sends two messages:

```ts
// plan-mode/index.ts (excerpt)
pi.sendMessage(planTodoListMessage, { deliverAs: "followUp" });
pi.sendMessage(
  { customType: "plan-mode-execute", content: execMessage, display: true },
  { triggerTurn: true, deliverAs: "followUp" },
);
```

Both options are needed, for different reasons from archetype 3's table:
`deliverAs: "followUp"` because the kickoff must wait for the current
turn (the one showing the plan) to finish rather than interrupt it, and
`triggerTurn: true` because after that turn the agent would be *idle* — and
an idle agent does not act on queued messages unless a turn is triggered.
Miss either one and execution either interrupts the plan display or never
starts.

**Verify the tour:** load `plan-mode/`, `/plan`, ask for a plan, choose
"Execute the plan", and watch: write tools disappear from the active set
(subsystem 1), a non-allowlisted `bash` command is blocked with the exit
instruction (2), `/reload` mid-execution restores mode, steps, and the
status widget (3, 5), and execution begins without you typing anything (6).

### Dynamic tool loading: register many, activate few {#dynamic-tool-loading-register-many-activate-few}

**Problem:** your extension ships dozens of tools, but sending every schema
on every request wastes context and confuses tool choice.

**Recipe:** register all tools up front, keep only a small **loader tool**
active, and let it activate relevant tools mid-turn.
`kimi-deferred-tools.ts` is a minimal working loader:

```ts
// kimi-deferred-tools.ts (excerpt)
pi.registerTool({
  name: "tool_search",
  // ... description, parameters ...
  async execute(_toolCallId, params) {
    // ...find matching registered-but-inactive tools for params.query...
    const active = pi.getActiveTools();
    const added = active.includes("Calculator") ? [] : ["Calculator"];
    if (added.length > 0) pi.setActiveTools([...active, ...added]);
    return {
      content: [{ type: "text", text: "Success. Found 1 matching tool(s)" }],
      details: { matches: ["Calculator"], added },
    };
  },
});

pi.on("session_start", () => {
  pi.setActiveTools(["tool_search"]); // everything else: registered, inactive
});
```

- **Registered ≠ active.** All tools exist; `session_start` narrows the
  active set to the loader, so only its schema costs context until the
  model asks for more.
- **The added names go into the loader's `details`.** When the change is
  purely additive, Pi records them on the tool result and exposes the new
  definitions before the next model request — with native deferred loading
  on models that support it, the normal active-tool list otherwise.
- **Additive only.** Removing tools mid-turn forfeits deferred loading and
  can invalidate the provider's cached prompt prefix.
- **Lazy tools rely on `description` alone.** Activating a tool that
  carries `promptSnippet`/`promptGuidelines` rebuilds the system prompt,
  which invalidates the prefix even when the provider supports deferred
  schemas. The shipped `dynamic-tools.ts` covers the simpler command-driven
  registration case.

**Verify:** load the example, prompt `use the available tools to calculate
100 + 500`, and observe the model call `tool_search`, then `Calculator` —
which was never in the initial active set.

### Replace the session safely {#replace-the-session-safely}

**Problem:** `ctx.newSession()`, `ctx.fork()`, `ctx.switchSession()`, and
`ctx.reload()` tear down the current runtime and spin up a new one. Your
handler keeps running in the old call frame, but every captured
session-bound object — `ctx.sessionManager`, `pi`, anything your
`session_shutdown` handler invalidated — now belongs to a dead runtime and
will throw or misbehave.

**Recipe:** do post-replacement work in the `withSession` callback, which
receives a fresh context bound to the replacement session, and capture only
plain data (strings, ids, serialized config) into it. `handoff.ts` — which
generates a handoff prompt, then opens a fresh session with that prompt
waiting in the editor — does exactly this:

```ts
// handoff.ts (excerpt)
const currentSessionFile = ctx.sessionManager.getSessionFile(); // plain data
const editedPrompt = await ctx.ui.editor("Edit handoff prompt", result);

const newSessionResult = await ctx.newSession({
  parentSession: currentSessionFile,
  withSession: async (replacementCtx) => {
    // Use only replacementCtx here — never the captured ctx or pi.
    replacementCtx.ui.setEditorText(editedPrompt);
    replacementCtx.ui.notify("Handoff ready. Submit when ready.", "info");
  },
});
```

- **`parentSession` is a string captured *before* the switch** — plain data
  survives; object references do not.
- **Everything after the switch uses `replacementCtx`** — the old `ctx` is
  a dead runtime's context, and touching it is the bug this pattern exists
  to prevent.
- Treat `await ctx.reload()` as terminal for its handler: `return`
  immediately after it, and put post-reload behavior in the newly loaded
  instance (for example its `session_start` handler).

**Verify:** run `/handoff <goal>` and confirm the generated prompt appears
in the *new* session's editor, with no errors referencing the old context.

### Talk between extensions (and a bug to find) {#talk-between-extensions}

**Problem:** one extension produces state another consumes, and neither
should import the other.

**Recipe:** `pi.events` is a shared event bus. Namespace your event names
(`my-ext:indexed`) so packages from different authors cannot collide. And
manage the subscription lifecycle — which the shipped `event-bus.ts`
itself gets *wrong*, a real bug we can learn from:

> **Spot the bug — `event-bus.ts` never unsubscribes.** It calls
> `pi.events.on("my:notification", ...)` at module top level. The event bus
> survives `/reload`; your extension instance does not. So every `/reload`
> adds another listener from the old instance, and each event fires every
> stale handler — you get duplicate notifications with stale closures.
>
> Try it: load the file, `/emit hello`, `/reload`, `/emit hello` again —
> the notification appears twice.
>
> The fix is the lifecycle pair from the file-trigger fix: subscribe in
> `session_start`, unsubscribe in `session_shutdown`:

```ts
let unsubscribe: (() => void) | undefined;

pi.on("session_start", () => {
  unsubscribe?.(); // defensive: drop any prior subscription
  unsubscribe = pi.events.on("my-ext:indexed", (data) => {
    // Handle the event.
  });
});

pi.on("session_shutdown", () => {
  unsubscribe?.();
  unsubscribe = undefined;
});

// Elsewhere (any extension): pi.events.emit("my-ext:indexed", { count: 17 });
```

**Failure mode:** events are ephemeral — not persisted, not replayed — and
`emit()` does not await asynchronous listeners, so never use the bus for
state that must survive or be acknowledged.

**Verify:** with the fix applied, `/emit hello`, `/reload`, `/emit hello` —
the handler fires exactly once per event.

### Evolve or override an existing tool {#evolve-or-override-an-existing-tool}

**Problem A — compatibility:** you tightened a tool's schema, and now
resuming an old session fails because a stored tool call's arguments no
longer validate.

**Recipe A:** `prepareArguments(args)` runs *before* schema validation and
before `execute()`. Fold legacy shapes into the modern one there, and strip
the legacy fields so what remains is exactly the current schema. Do not add
deprecated compatibility fields to `parameters` — that also teaches the
model the legacy shape.

```ts
prepareArguments(args) {
  if (!args || typeof args !== "object") return args;
  const { oldText, newText, ...rest } = args as {
    oldText?: unknown; newText?: unknown;
    edits?: Array<{ oldText: string; newText: string }>;
  };
  if (typeof oldText !== "string" || typeof newText !== "string") {
    return args; // nothing to shim; validation will judge it
  }
  // Modern shape only: legacy fields folded in and removed.
  return { ...rest, edits: [...(rest.edits ?? []), { oldText, newText }] };
},
```

**Problem B — behavior:** you need `read`, `bash`, or another built-in to
behave differently for every model call — redact secrets from `read`
output, route `bash` through a sandbox.

**Recipe B:** register a tool with the same name. `tool-override.ts`
overrides `read` with access logging and blocked-path checks. Three
contracts keep an override invisible to the rest of Pi:

1. **Preserve the built-in result shape**, including the `details` type —
   the UI and session logic depend on it. (Note honestly: `tool-override.ts`
   itself diverges here — it returns `{ lines: number }` where built-in
   `read` returns `{ truncation: ... }`. Nothing breaks today because its
   renderers are inherited, but any downstream code reading
   `details.truncation` would get `undefined`. Treat the example as a demo
   of the mechanism, and preserve the documented shape in your own
   overrides.)
2. **Renderer inheritance is per slot**: omit `renderCall` and Pi reuses
   the built-in one; same for `renderResult`. `tool-override.ts` omits
   both, so syntax highlighting and line numbers keep working unchanged.
3. **Prompt metadata is not inherited** — redefine `promptSnippet` and
   `promptGuidelines` if the override should keep them.

Built-in tools also accept pluggable `operations` (`ReadOperations`,
`BashOperations`, ...) for remote execution — the shipped `ssh.ts` routes
all tools to a remote machine this way, and `user_bash` can route the
interactive `!`/`!!` shell through the same backends.

**Failure mode:** prefer an archetype-1 guard when blocking or observing is
enough; override only when the result itself must change.

**Verify:** for A, resume a session containing a legacy-shape call and
confirm it validates and executes. For B, confirm the transcript renders
exactly as before, then confirm the new behavior.

**When you outgrow one session:** `subagent/` is the largest shipped
composition — a tool that delegates tasks to specialized agents in isolated
`pi` subprocesses, with streaming, parallel execution, and abort
propagation. Read it after the patterns above are familiar.

## Deploy and share

Pi configuration is layered — built-in defaults, global settings under
`~/.pi/agent`, project settings under `.pi`, CLI flags and environment, then
extension behavior at runtime — and narrower layers win. When a setting "does
not apply", check which layer set the value you are actually getting. Use
`CONFIG_DIR_NAME` instead of hardcoding `.pi` when constructing project paths
(rebranded distributions can rename it), and call `ctx.isProjectTrusted()`
before honoring project-local configuration of your own — trust is an
input-loading decision, not a sandbox for subsequent tool execution.
[Resources, settings, and trust](#sec:resources) is the canonical guide.

A minimal shareable [package](#sec:glossary) is a directory with a
`package.json` declaring its resources in a `pi` manifest:

```json
{
  "name": "@myteam/pi-tools",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "peerDependencies": {
    "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent": "*"
  },
  "pi": {
    "extensions": ["./extensions"]
  }
}
```

Manifest fields, dependency placement, install commands, and publishing steps
are in [Packaging and sharing extensions](#sec:packages).

Provider configuration can expose credentials: keep API keys in environment
references and never log headers, payloads, or system-prompt options. For
`pi.registerProvider()` and provider internals, see [Models, providers, and
authentication](#sec:models); for custom components, editors, and keybindings,
see [Terminal UI and interactive mode](#sec:tui) — never hardcode a raw key
check in extension code.

### Pattern-specific mistakes

General first-extension pitfalls (loading, naming, discovery) are in [Your
first extension](#sec:extensions); exact event contracts are in the [Extension
event reference](#sec:events). This table keeps only mistakes tied to this
chapter's patterns:

| Mistake | Why it fails | Better approach |
|---|---|---|
| Keep all extension state in a closure | Reload/resume/fork loses it | Rebuild from the active branch ([durable state](#state-that-survives-restart-and-branching)) |
| Rebuild state from `getEntries()` | Scans dead sibling branches into the current state | `getBranch()` follows the active path only ([rebuild loop](#state-that-survives-restart-and-branching)) |
| Snapshot state only on success paths | An error result breaks the rebuild chain | Snapshot in *every* result's `details` ([snapshot design](#state-that-survives-restart-and-branching)) |
| Use `sendMessage` for private metadata | The model receives it | `appendEntry` (+ entry renderer if it should render) ([delivery modes](#messages-entries-and-delivery-modes)) |
| `sendMessage` while idle without `triggerTurn` | Message queues silently; nothing runs | `triggerTurn: true` ([delivery modes](#messages-entries-and-delivery-modes)) |
| Start `fs.watch`/timers in `session_start` without cleanup | Every `/reload` adds another, holding a stale runtime | Close in `session_shutdown` ([spot the bug](#messages-entries-and-delivery-modes)) |
| Use captured `ctx`/`pi`/`sessionManager` after replacement | They belong to the torn-down runtime | `withSession` with plain captured data ([session replacement](#replace-the-session-safely)) |
| Ignore `AbortSignal` in a tool (`execSync`!) | Esc cannot stop your nested work | Forward `signal`; async spawn over `execSync` ([execute core](#tool-execute-core)) |
| Mutate a file without the queue | Parallel siblings lose writes | `withFileMutationQueue` around the whole window ([file queue](#serialize-same-file-mutations)) |
| Change the built-in result shape in an override | UI/session code depends on it | Preserve the documented `details` contract ([override](#evolve-or-override-an-existing-tool)) |
| Subscribe to `pi.events` without unsubscribing | Every `/reload` adds a stale listener | Unsubscribe in `session_shutdown` ([events](#talk-between-extensions)) |
| Activate lazy tools with prompt metadata | System-prompt rebuild invalidates the cache prefix | Description-only lazy tools ([dynamic loading](#dynamic-tool-loading-register-many-activate-few)) |
| Hardcode the tool list in `setActiveTools` | Destroys other extensions' tools | Filter/union the saved selection ([plan-mode tour](#the-plan-mode-tour)) |
| Assume tool hooks observe sibling results | Parallel tools finish independently | Persist/coordinate after the batch or avoid the dependency |
| Assume `agent_end` means completely idle | Retry, compaction, or queued work may still run | Use `agent_settled` or `waitForIdle()` ([prompt lifecycle](#sec:prompt-lifecycle)) |
| Write to stdout with `console.log` | It corrupts print, JSON, and RPC output | Use notifications or the debug log ([run modes](#sec:modes)) |
| Test only `pi -e` | It does not prove discovery/reload behavior | Auto-discovery plus `/reload` ([verification ladder](#a-practical-verification-ladder)) |

### A practical verification ladder {#a-practical-verification-ladder}

Use evidence appropriate to what you changed:

1. Type-check the extension with the same TypeScript version/API contracts used
   by Pi, especially tool parameters and event return values. From an extension
   package with a `tsconfig.json`, run `npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json`.
2. Load it with `pi -e path/to/extension.ts` to isolate load errors.
3. Move it to an auto-discovered location — for example
   `~/.pi/agent/extensions/my-extension.ts` — restart Pi, and verify
   `session_start` ran (add a temporary `ctx.ui.notify` or debug-log line).
4. Exercise the happy path and the relevant failure/deny/cancel path.
5. Run `/reload` in the session, then repeat step 4. Confirm no duplicate
   resource, stale closure, or leaked status remains.
6. For persistence, exit and start a new process, resume with `pi --resume`
   (or fork with `/fork` inside the session), and verify the
   intended branch state is restored.
7. For tools, test a malformed call/schema failure and a cancellation. For
   mutating tools, test concurrent sibling calls if applicable.
8. If you change repository code, run `npm run check` and the relevant targeted
   test rather than a real-provider test. The coding-agent suite uses a faux
   provider and `test/suite/harness.ts` for deterministic tests; as covered in
   [Testing, debugging, and contribution workflow](#sec:testing), the
   faux-provider harness is also the practical way to test an extension's
   behavior without real API keys.

### Examples by archetype

The repository ships runnable versions of everything in this chapter under
`packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/`. Start with the smallest match:

- **Guards:** `permission-gate.ts`, `protected-paths.ts`,
  `confirm-destructive.ts`, `timed-confirm.ts`, `prompt-customizer.ts`
- **Tools:** `truncated-tool.ts`, `question.ts` (tool with user dialogs)
- **Stateful:** `todo.ts`, `entry-renderer.ts`, `file-trigger.ts`,
  `send-user-message.ts`
- **Composers:** `plan-mode/`, `preset.ts`, `kimi-deferred-tools.ts`,
  `dynamic-tools.ts`, `handoff.ts`, `event-bus.ts`, `tool-override.ts`,
  `subagent/`

## Try it

1. **(Guard)** Build the gate across all three guard sections: load
   `permission-gate.ts`, add the `timeout` option from `timed-confirm.ts`,
   and test approve, deny, timeout-deny, and the `pi -p` fallback. Then
   write one steering rule with `before_agent_start` and verify it changes
   behavior without blocking anything.
2. **(Tool)** Write a small real tool of your own and pass it through the
   six layers: schema with real descriptions, `ctx.cwd`-relative execution,
   the throw-vs-return rule, `truncateHead` with a temp-file spill, compact
   renderers, and `withFileMutationQueue` for any file writes. Test a
   malformed call, an oversized result, and two same-file edits in one
   turn.
3. **(Stateful)** Run the full todo.ts lifecycle script from pass 2 —
   add todos, `/reload`, `/fork`, add one more, `/tree` back and forth,
   quit, `pi --resume` — and confirm the list matches the active branch at
   every step. Then explain, in one sentence each, why the rebuild uses
   `getBranch()` and why error results carry snapshots.
4. **(Composer)** Do the event-bus bug hunt end to end: load the shipped
   `event-bus.ts`, `/emit hello`, `/reload`, `/emit hello`, count the
   notifications, then apply the subscribe/unsubscribe fix and confirm
   exactly one. As a stretch, recreate a mini plan-mode: a `/readonly`
   command that saves the active tools, removes `edit`/`write`, gates
   `bash` through an allowlist whose block reason explains how to exit,
   and persists the mode with `appendEntry`.
